courses.title: Jewish life in exile and the wider world
courses.description: Six sessions in historical context, communal institutions, memory, translation, and responsible comparison.

sessions.title: Locate Jeremiah's audience
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
choices: Who is addressed, in what setting, and for what purpose?
Which of today's political debates does the verse settle?
What later doctrines can be built directly on this line?
sessions.explanation: Historical reading begins with speaker, audience, setting, and purpose — not with the modern uses a verse might be recruited for.

sessions.title: Read exile as a setting
sessions.translation: To which I have exiled you.
choices: It shapes the communal question the verse is answering.
It reduces the verse to a mere marker of when it was written.
It fixes the meaning so tightly that no later reading applies.
sessions.explanation: Context is evidence for reading, not a replacement for the source — exile frames the question without freezing or emptying the verse.

sessions.title: Compare rabbinic worlds
sessions.prompt: What can this comparison help explain?
choices: How communities, language, and institutions shape the questions asked.
How two distant communities came to read their texts identically.
How a text's meaning stays fixed regardless of where it is studied.
sessions.explanation: Texts are studied by communities in particular places — the comparison shows how place shapes reading, not how it drops out.

sessions.title: Name an institution
sessions.prompt: What does this cluster invite a learner to study?
choices: How learning, law, and belonging take on lasting social form.
The precise dictionary definition of each of the three terms.
How ideas develop entirely apart from any community that holds them.
sessions.explanation: Institutions sustain and reshape learning across time — the cluster points to social form, not vocabulary drills or ideas without communities.

sessions.title: Treat memory as evidence
choices: A source is evidence about an event and about how it was remembered.
A source is a neutral record that simply reports what took place.
A source shaped by memory has no real value for the historian.
sessions.explanation: Sources are both windows and voices — neither a neutral camera nor worthless once memory has shaped them.

sessions.title: Compare without flattening
sessions.prompt: What makes a wider-world comparison responsible?
choices: Name a shared question and preserve each source's context and difference.
Assume that traditions using similar words are essentially interchangeable.
Begin from a general impression of what each tradition is like.
sessions.explanation: Comparison is disciplined close reading across distinct worlds — it preserves difference rather than flattening it or starting from a stereotype.

production.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
